name: Minimally Invasive Surgery, Pneumoperitoneum Physiology, and Laparoscopy

reference.source: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22nd ed / SAGES Manual
clinicalPearls: Carbon dioxide is the insufflation gas of choice because of its high blood solubility, rapid pulmonary clearance, and non-combustibility
Pneumoperitoneum increases systemic vascular resistance and intra-abdominal pressure while reducing venous return and cardiac index
Venous gas embolism during laparoscopy produces a classic mill-wheel murmur, sudden drop in end-tidal CO2, and hemodynamic collapse
Management of acute gas embolism mandates immediate desufflation, Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus, Trendelenburg), and 100% oxygen
Palmer point in the left midclavicular subcostal margin serves as a safe alternative entry site in patients with prior midline laparotomies
reference.pathophysiology: Peritoneal insufflation with carbon dioxide to standard working pressures of 12 to 15 mmHg elevates diaphragm position, reduces pulmonary compliance, and elevates peak airway pressures. Systemic absorption of CO2 induces hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis, compensated by hyperventilation. Increased intra-abdominal pressure compresses the inferior vena cava and splanchnic circulation, elevating afterload and diminishing cardiac output. Direct trocar insertion injuries can lacerate the abdominal aorta, common iliac vessels, or bowel, requiring immediate conversion to open laparotomy.
additionalDifferentials: Carbon dioxide gas embolism versus tension pneumothorax during upper abdominal laparoscopy
Hypovolemic shock from occult trocar vessel injury versus vasovagal reflex from peritoneal stretch
Capacitive coupling diathermy bowel burn versus direct mechanical trocar injury
Postoperative diaphragmatic phrenic nerve referred pain versus acute subdiaphragmatic peritonitis
additionalInvestigations: Continuous capnography monitoring for sudden drop in end-tidal carbon dioxide
Arterial blood gas analysis to assess respiratory acidosis and arterial oxygenation
Diagnostic laparoscopy with visual inspection of all trocar sites upon cannula removal
Abdominal CT with oral and IV contrast for delayed postoperative bowel perforation
